newsitem.title: USA: Motorola Q4 results show signs of recovery.
newsitem.headline: Motorola Q4 results show signs of recovery.

text.p: Motorola Inc gave analysts hope that a turnaround is on the way for the technology giant by reporting what appear to be better-than-expected fourth quarter results and a rebound in orders in its key businesses.
"It looks like they certainly seem to be on the ramp to recovery," said Rakesh Sood, an analyst for Hambrecht & Quist.
Motorola Thursday posted fourth quarter net earnings of $0.39 a share versus $0.72 a share last year. The results included more than $150 million in restructuring costs and "other unusual charges."
According to First Call, the consensus of analysts' estimates was $0.41 a share, with a range of $0.35 to $0.45, but only some analysts said they included estimated charges.
Excluding the charges, analysts calculated that Motorola earned $0.55 a share -- topping all estimates on Wall Street.
"The real operating number is $0.55," said Mona Eraiba, an analyst for Gruntal & Co. "The highest on the Street was myself at $0.48...This is great news."
Analysts said they were impressed with overall sales for the fourth quarter, which rose to $7.7 billion from $7.3 billion. They said they had expected sales to fall.
"These results were really better than expected," said Douglas Christopher, an analyst for Crowell, Weedon & Co. "No one thought sales would be that good."

Motorola's semiconductor sales, which in 1995 accounted for some 29 percent of the company's overall revenues, fell from 1995's fourth quarter. The industry has been hit with over-capacity and has only recently begun to pick up.
But analysts said new orders were up 24 percent in the fourth quarter 1996 compared with the third, which was key.
"That's bigger than I thought," Eraiba said. "I had thought (there was) only a little bounce."
In addition, analysts said Motorola's book-to-bill ratio for semiconductors was 1.0 indicating new orders were equal to shipments, compared with a negative 0.82 in the third quarter.
"It's a big sequential improvement from the previous quarter," Eraiba said.

Motorola's General Systems Segment, which includes wireless phone infrastructure and handsets, also showed positive signs, analysts said, with sales up 17 percent from last year. Handsets in particular have been plagued with stiff competition and pricing pressure.
"Competitive pressures do remain, but they have at least bottomed out," Sood said, adding the segment was helped by sales of infrastructure and the recently introduced StarTAC phone.
Last year, General Systems accounted for about 36 percent of the company's overall sales.
Analysts said they would ask for more information on the charges during a conference call with the company scheduled for 0700 CST/1300 GMT Friday.
"I don't know the breakout of all the charges, but it looks like operations have improved," Eraiba said. "We wanted them to take the hit and move forward."
